🚨 TRUMP v. CLINTON — RUSSIAGATE RETURNS TO THE SUPREME COURT

A significant development in the years-long legal battle over the origins of the Trump–Russia investigation.

On October 21, the Supreme Court distributed President Trump’s petition for consideration at its November 6 conference, potentially opening the door to review of his dismissed lawsuit against Hillary Clinton and numerous other defendants.

THE BACKSTORY:

In March 2022, Trump filed a sweeping civil lawsuit alleging that Hillary Clinton, the DNC, Fusion GPS, Christopher Steele, and others participated in a coordinated effort to falsely associate his 2016 presidential campaign with Russia.

The lawsuit included allegations involving:

• The Clinton campaign’s funding of opposition research that produced the Steele dossier.

• The dissemination of allegations concerning Trump and Russia to journalists and federal authorities.

• Alleged coordination among political operatives, researchers, attorneys and others to damage Trump’s campaign, presidency and business interests.

• Alleged violations of federal racketeering laws (RICO), along with additional state-law claims.

HOW DID WE GET HERE?

2022: Federal Judge Donald Middlebrooks dismissed Trump’s lawsuit, finding serious legal deficiencies, including expired statutes of limitations and insufficiently supported claims.

2023: The judge imposed approximately $938,000 in sanctions against Trump and attorney Alina Habba, finding that the litigation was frivolous and brought in bad faith. Additional sanctions were imposed in related proceedings.

November 2025: The 11th Circuit Court of Appeals largely upheld the dismissal and sanctions.

May 2026: Trump’s request for rehearing was denied.

July–August 2026: Justice Clarence Thomas granted two extensions allowing Trump’s attorneys additional time to prepare their Supreme Court petition.

October 9: Trump formally petitioned the Supreme Court to review the case.

October 19: Clinton and other respondents waived their right to submit an initial response.

October 21: The petition was distributed for the Supreme Court’s November 6 conference.

HERE’S THE IMPORTANT LEGAL DISTINCTION:

Trump’s attorneys argue that his constitutional responsibilities as president justified suspending the statute of limitations on his private civil claims while he was serving his first term.

They also challenge the sanctions imposed for advancing that argument.

In other words, the Supreme Court is being asked to consider whether the lower courts improperly prevented Trump’s claims from proceeding and penalized his attorneys for their legal arguments.

WHY THE TIMING IS INTERESTING:

This is unfolding alongside renewed scrutiny of the origins of Russiagate, including declassification developments and allegations concerning how the Trump–Russia narrative was constructed.

We’ve been following these developments for months as part of a broader resurgence of controversies originating between 2016 and 2020.

Now the original Trump–Clinton civil litigation has reached the Supreme Court’s doorstep.

THE BIG QUESTION:

Could a Supreme Court ruling create an opportunity for Trump to pursue claims that were previously dismissed?

But on November 6, they’ll consider whether this legal battle warrants Supreme Court review.

SCOTUS Case No. 26-518
